paragraphs.text: Just how important is a construction material such as concrete? Not highly valued by the vast majority of the population, the material has become synonymous with the words 'inferior', 'cheap' – and even 'inhuman'. And when looking at some of the decaying 20th-century tower blocks in inner-city areas, it is difficult to disagree.

What would be wrong, though, would be to blame these housing disasters on the material itself, rather than on the planning philosophy adopted when they were being built, a philosophy that was keen to house people in buildings that had been constructed quickly. without much care and attention, using unproven systems. There was no maintenance programme put in place, and as a consequence the buildings slowly decayed.

It is now time that concrete was forgiven and rehabilitated, especially now that the international design community is beginning to experiment more with the new techniques and ideas surrounding this ancient material. To design successfully in concrete is to understand the material from a structural point of view, and the architects who love it, understand it, and experiment with it work closely with engineers to develop their designs. Concrete isn't actually a cheaper option when compared with wood or stone – in fact, well-crafted concrete can be very expensive – but it is more environmentally sustainable. It can be restored, re-polished, and re-varnished and, if looked after, concrete can last for hundreds, if not thousands of years.

It was in the second century BC that the Romans first quarried pink, sand-like material from Pozzuoli, Italy. Initially mistaken for sand, this fine, volcanic ash contained silica and alumina One of the first large-scale uses of this material was in the theatre of Pompeii, constructed in 75 BC. Concrete was mainly used for the foundations and, because it had no strength under tension without other elements being added to it, it was used to fill in the gaps between the main building materials of bricks and stones. Attempts were made to reinforce concrete with bronze, but this was only partially successful because the bronze reacted to higher and lower temperatures at a different rate to concrete, and this caused the concrete to crack.

Depending on how it is used, reinforced concrete can be as strong as steel under tension and cope with as much pressure as stone. When concrete first emerged as a possible material for the construction of long-span structures, such as bridges, it was assumed to have the same limitations as wood or steel – the possibilities of what could be achieved with concrete were not immediately clear. However, through experimentation over decades, concrete's great strength has allowed it to be used for practically all types of major engineering projects, including the construction of lighthouses, high-rise buildings, roads, bridges, sea-barriers and dams.

Modern concrete comes in many forms and is only as strong as what it's made from. Essentially it is a mix of calcium and silicates extracted from calcareous and sedimentary rocks, such as chalk and clay, which, when combined with other ingredients, form a powder called cement. Adding water causes a chemical reaction – known as hydration – which sets and hardens the cement and turns it into concrete. This process can take a long time, thus increasing the strength of the concrete over a period of perhaps many months.

The mix of the ingredients is therefore vital to concrete's structural properties. The proportion of water added to the concrete mix is critical in determining how water resistant it is, as well as its strength and resistance to weather and wear. Too high a percentage of water dilutes the cement paste and weakens the chemical bonds between the different ingredients resulting in a weak concrete. Concrete mixes are described in terms of the proportions of their constituent materials. The mix is specified according to the required strength appearance, durability, and workability of the finished product. By altering the proportions of the different ingredients, changes can be made to the properties of both the fresh and hardened concrete.

A range of properties can be added to the fresh concrete through the use of special ingredients - accelerators to increase the speed at which it hardens, for example, and retarders to slow it down. In some cases, plasticizers are also added to the mix, allowing it to flow well, without the need to add extra water. It is also possible to add an ingredient to the concrete mixture which introduces small bubbles that help the hardened concrete resist the destructive contraction and expansion of the material brought about by repeated freezing and thawing. This allows the concrete to be used in areas where there are extremes of temperatures.

Simply by changing the type of rock used, concrete can be made so light that it can float on water, or made so heavy that it is almost twice its usual density. Concrete can be made totally resistant to moisture for use in the construction of gigantic dams, or porous enough to allow liquid to flow through it as in sewage treatment plants, where filter beds made out of concrete cleanse and purify the water.
